answer:
Market attractiveness: The broader prescription savings market is large and validated (GoodRx-style discount cards, pharmacy and insurer apps, mail-order generics), which proves willingness to pay for price transparency. But that same validation signals a crowded, commoditizing space where incumbents have scale, pharmacy/PBM relationships, brand recognition and distribution that a student team cannot match. Market attractiveness is moderate overall, but the specific wedge chosen is less attractive than the headline market.

Is this the right target group? The 18-34 chronic-condition segment is a defensible and sympathetic niche with a real pain point (new to managing costs, high-deductible or gig-work coverage, cost-driven non-adherence). However, there are structural weaknesses as a monetization target: (1) young adults tend to be on low-cost generics, so absolute savings per user, and therefore referral fees per fill, are small; (2) they have low income and low willingness to pay for subscriptions, which makes the premium tier a weak revenue source; (3) the segment is lower-utilization than older cohorts, so engagement frequency is limited to monthly refills; and (4) the segment is not defensible, since GoodRx and others already serve these users and can add budgeting or tailored education cheaply. The segment is a good go-to-market beachhead for acquisition and community trust, but a poor stand-alone business. The team has also not validated demand beyond a small, convenience-sampled student group, and has not measured savings or retention, so the 'correct group' claim is unproven.

Market size and scalability: The plan only says 'several million' people, unrefined. Even taking 3-5M users as addressable, realistic revenue per user is low: referral fees of a few dollars per fill at best, only on fills that convert through the app, and subscription at a few dollars per month with low conversion. A rough view of a few million addressable users, low single-digit penetration and perhaps tens of dollars of annual revenue per active user implies a niche business in the single-digit to low tens of millions in revenue even in an optimistic case, not a venture-scale outcome. Scaling would require expanding to all demographics, which puts the company in direct competition with entrenched, well-funded players, or expanding into B2B/B2B2C (campus health centers, employers, clinics), which the team has not tested. The secondary markets are plausible and may be better revenue sources (employer benefits, health systems, payers interested in adherence), but they carry long sales cycles and regulatory and privacy burdens (HIPAA, data licensing).

Exit potential: Realistic exits are acqui-hire or tuck-in acquisition by a larger discount-card player, pharmacy chain, PBM, digital health or fintech-for-health company seeking Gen Z/young adult users or a budgeting layer, or a campus/benefits platform. Such exits are likely modest in size unless the company demonstrates strong retention, proprietary data, or a unique distribution channel. Independent IPO or large venture-scale exit is unlikely on the current positioning. Exit value hinges on proving measurable savings, adherence improvement and retention, and on securing referral/data partnerships, none of which exist yet. Referral economics also depend on pharmacy/discount provider agreements that are unsigned and where the company has little bargaining power.

Overall assessment: The market is real and the problem genuine, so the venture could support a small, sustainable business or a niche acquisition. It is not yet evidence of a large, scalable, venture-backed market. Key risks are thin unit economics, weak differentiation against well-capitalized incumbents, dependence on third-party price data and partners, and an unrefined market sizing. To strengthen the case, the team should quantify the addressable market bottom-up (users x fills x referral fee), measure average savings per user and retention in the pilot, test one B2B channel (campus health or employer), and show a path to expand beyond the beachhead segment without head-on competition.
